Claims of autism were the big thing that made news a few years ago, but I don't know if that was actually substantiated. I've seen a lot of people claim it wasn't.

Things people don't like about vaccines:

They usually contain mercury, aluminum, formaldehyde, fetal cells from humans and animals, and other stuff that you generally wouldn't want to put into your body.

The blood/brain barrier is not fully developed until 2 years of age, and vaccine recommendations begin at 2 months.

Testing for safety of ingredient dosing, as well as safety of whole vaccines seems lacking. For instance, the flu shot and TDaP are currently being pushed really hard for pregnant women, but no safety testing has been done on pregnant humans, and little if any safety testing has been done on pregnant animals. Any other medication with that status is recommended against, but these are heavily pushed.

Data on the frequency of people having bad reactions/harm from vaccines is hard to find. Even if reported, they are often brushed off as unrelated, even if it's a known side effect. People with really bad reactions (like fatal allergic reactions, or chronic illness) usually end up with settlements that include gag orders. There are warning labels for all vaccines that list potential side effects, which people generally are not made aware of, but it's available to read.

I've also heard claims of the flu shot increasing rates of female infertility and miscarriage, but I haven't seen data on it.

There's also the question of whether a particular vaccine actually makes the person who gets it immune. I haven't found a good place to look for efficacy rates, and I wonder if it's because people don't get tested to confirm immunity that much.

Some vaccines reliably impart immunity, but it can also wear off over time. For example, the TDap is tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis, and the pertussis immunity wears off in two years at most, but they give you the whole thing for each booster. Each booster for pertussis is less effective and wears off faster than the last, as well. The outbreaks of pertussis (whooping cough) in recent years have actually largely been among vaccinated children, because of how quickly the immunity wears off.

Overall, I think there's plenty of negatives to think about, and I'm not sure what route I'll personally take with my children. The rates of serious side effects are pretty low, unless they're much better at hiding them than I suspect, and many of the diseases can be fatal or have very serious side effects, like deafness from measles. Imo, it's about relative risk for each particular vaccine, I'm not planning to pick and choose which ones to get and when and disregard the recommended schedule.
